title: Event Decoration & Styling
subtitle: Plan, price and set up safe, beautiful decor for weddings, birthdays and church events, on time and within budget.
description: A practical course for decorating Nigerian celebrations: turning a client's wishes into a clear colour scheme and design, building balloon garlands, backdrops, draping and table settings, and pricing the job with a proper quotation and deposit. You also learn to plan the event morning backwards from guest arrival, work safely with candles and electrics, and build a portfolio that wins the next job.
outcomes: Run a client brief and venue check, and turn vague wishes into an approved written design
Build colour schemes with the 60-30-10 rule and one clear focal point
Build an organic balloon garland, a draped backdrop and consistent table settings, and calculate the materials needed
Write an itemised quotation with contingency, profit, deposit and balance terms, and decide what to rent or buy
Plan an event-day timeline and setup safely with candles, electrics, heights and outdoor wind
Document a full project and present a portfolio and service packages to clients
audience: Women who already enjoy decorating for family and church events and want to offer reliable, paid decoration services.
tools: Smartphone with camera, WhatsApp (ideally WhatsApp Business) and a free design app such as Canva
Tape measure, notebook or Google Sheets
Balloon pump and sizer, garland strip, glue dots, cable ties, fishing line
Scissors, clips, pins, gaffer tape, a step ladder
Extension box with surge protection and flameless candles
Access to an event rental company for cloths, chair covers and frames

modules.title: Foundations: the decorator's job, design basics and readiness
modules.overview: Understand what an event decorator actually delivers, the main event types you will serve in Nigeria, and the design basics that make a hall look planned instead of crowded. You finish the module with a written readiness plan, a starter kit list and the safety rules you will follow at every job.

lessons.title: What an event decorator delivers, and the jobs you can start with
objectives: Describe the four things a client is really paying a decorator for
Name the main decoration zones in a Nigerian wedding, birthday or church event
Compare small, medium and large jobs and pick a sensible first job size
List the stages of a decoration job from first enquiry to pack-down

blocks.text: An event decorator turns an ordinary space, such as a church hall, a hotel ballroom, a canopy on a compound or a living room, into a setting that matches one occasion. The client is not only buying balloons and fabric. They are paying for four things: **a look** that suits the event, **reliability** (everything ready before guests arrive), **safety** (nothing falls, burns or trips anyone) and **peace of mind** (they do not have to think about decor on a stressful day).

blocks.name: special-event
blocks.alt: A person preparing a decorated space for a special event
blocks.caption: Your product is a finished, safe, on-time setting, not just a pile of decorations.

blocks.text: The events you will decorate most
In Nigeria the steady work comes from a few event types. Each one has its own rhythm and its own pressure points, so it helps to know them before you price anything.

head: Event
Typical decor zones
What the client worries about
rows: Couple's seat or stage, family seating, gift area, canopy or hall entrance
Colours matching the families' aso ebi, space for cultural rites
High table, backdrop, guest tables with centrepieces, entrance, cake table
Elegance, photos, finishing before the couple's grand entrance
Balloon garland or arch, photo backdrop, cake table, dessert or souvenir table
Theme, colours, a good photo spot, budget
Altar or pulpit area, stage, entrance, reception tables
Respect for the church's rules, quick setup between services
Stage backdrop, registration table, branding, guest tables

blocks.text: Small, medium and large jobs

Think of jobs by **size and risk**, not just by money. A small job is a home birthday with one balloon garland, a backdrop and a cake table, set up in two to three hours by you and one helper. A medium job is a 100 to 200 guest party or church reception with tablecloths, centrepieces, a backdrop and an entrance, needing four to six hours and two or three helpers. A large job is a wedding reception for several hundred guests with ceiling draping, a stage, lighting and many tables, often needing a crew and a setup that starts the night before.

Start where a mistake is survivable. If a balloon garland at a home birthday comes out uneven, you can fix it in twenty minutes. If you misjudge the setup time for a 400 guest wedding, there is no fixing it once the couple arrives. Most successful decorators grow by doing many small jobs very well, collecting photos and referrals, and only then taking on bigger halls.

blocks.title: Partner before you buy
blocks.text: Many decorators begin by working as a paid helper for an established decorator. You learn setup speed, crew roles and how to handle clients, and you see which items are worth owning before spending your own money.
The life of one decoration job

Every job, small or large, follows the same path. Knowing the stages lets you explain your process to clients and stops you skipping the boring steps that protect you, such as the written agreement and the deposit.

blocks.title: From enquiry to pack-down
items: Enquiry and client brief
Venue check and design
Quotation and deposit
Prepare, buy, rent
Setup and final walkthrough
Pack-down and feedback
blocks.caption: Skipping any stage, especially the deposit or the venue check, is where most decoration problems begin.

blocks.title: Worked example: sizing up a first enquiry
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi in Enugu receives a WhatsApp message: a mother wants decor for her daughter's 7th birthday at home, about 40 guests, pink and white, two weeks away.
steps: She asks three questions first: where exactly is the party, how much space is there (indoor sitting room or compound), and what budget range the mother has in mind.
The mother sends a video of the compound and says she is thinking about ₦150,000 to ₦200,000 (approximate).
Ngozi classifies it as a small job: one balloon garland on a backdrop stand, a cake table, and a simple welcome sign.
She estimates two and a half hours of setup with one helper and blocks the morning of the party in her calendar.
blocks.result: Within ten minutes Ngozi knows the job is within her ability, roughly what it will involve and whether the budget is realistic, before she spends any time on design.

blocks.text: Where decorators find their first clients

Your first jobs usually come from people who already know you: family, church members, colleagues and neighbours. Post clear photos of every setup on your WhatsApp Status and Instagram, with the event type and colours in the caption, never the client's private details. Introduce yourself to cake makers, caterers, photographers and event halls near you. These vendors are asked "do you know a decorator?" every week, and a vendor who has seen you arrive early and leave the hall clean will recommend you.

In the rest of this course you will build every stage: understanding the brief, choosing colours and materials, quoting with a deposit, planning logistics, setting up safely, and building a portfolio that wins the next job.

takeaways: Clients pay for a look, reliability, safety and peace of mind.
Each event type has its own decor zones and worries.
Start with small jobs where mistakes can be fixed, then grow.
Every job follows the same stages: brief, design, quote, prepare, set up, pack down.

activity.title: Map your local event market
steps: List five events you attended or saw in the last year (weddings, birthdays, church events).
For each, write the decor zones you remember: entrance, backdrop, tables, stage.
Mark each one small, medium or large using this lesson's descriptions.
Circle the one type you could confidently decorate first, and write why.
activity.evidence: A one-page note or phone photo of your event list with your chosen starting job type circled.

lessons.title: Colour schemes, focal points and balance that look planned
objectives: Build monochrome, analogous and complementary colour schemes using a colour wheel
Apply the 60-30-10 proportion rule to a decor plan
Choose one clear focal point for a room and support it
Match decor colours to aso ebi and a client's theme

blocks.text: The difference between decor that looks expensive and decor that looks busy is rarely money. It is usually **colour control** and **one clear focal point**. A hall with three well-chosen colours, repeated everywhere, looks planned. A hall with seven colours scattered around looks confused, even if each item is beautiful.

blocks.name: color-palette
blocks.alt: A person choosing colours from a palette
blocks.caption: Pick the palette first, then choose every balloon, fabric and flower to fit it.

blocks.text: Three colour schemes every decorator uses

A **colour wheel** arranges colours in a circle: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple, and the shades between them. You can find free colour wheel tools on your phone, such as Adobe Color in the browser. Three simple schemes cover most events.

head: Scheme
How to build it
Event example
rows: One colour in light, medium and dark shades, plus white or a neutral
Blush, rose and deep pink with white for a girl's birthday
Two or three colours sitting next to each other on the wheel
Gold, orange and burnt orange for a traditional wedding
Two colours opposite each other on the wheel, one dominant
Royal blue with gold accents for a thanksgiving service

blocks.text: Metallics such as gold, silver and rose gold behave like neutrals. They sit happily with most schemes and add shine under lights. White, ivory and cream also act as calm backgrounds that let your main colours stand out.
The 60-30-10 rule

Interior designers use a simple proportion guide called the **60-30-10 rule**: about 60 percent of what the eye sees is the main colour, about 30 percent is a second colour, and about 10 percent is an accent. It is a guide, not a law, but it stops a room from looking evenly split and flat.

blocks.title: 60-30-10 colour balance
items: 10% accent: gold details
30% secondary: champagne fabric
60% main: white base
blocks.caption: The biggest surfaces carry the main colour; small details carry the accent.

blocks.text: In a hall the big surfaces are tablecloths, chair covers, wall or ceiling drapes and the backdrop. These carry your 60 percent. Table runners, chair sashes and balloon clusters often carry the 30 percent. Napkin rings, candle holders, flowers and small props carry the 10 percent accent.
One focal point, supported

Every room needs one place where eyes go first. At a wedding reception it is usually the high table and backdrop. At a birthday it is the cake table with its balloon garland. At a church event it is the altar or stage. Spend the largest share of your effort and budget there, keep the guest tables simpler, and use the entrance to give guests a first taste of the colours.

blocks.title: Aso ebi comes first
blocks.text: At many Nigerian weddings the families choose aso ebi colours early. Ask for photos of the actual fabric, not just the colour name, because "wine" or "champagne" can mean very different shades. Build your palette to sit well with the fabric guests will wear, so photos look unified.

blocks.title: Worked example: turning a vague request into a palette
blocks.context: For example, Funke is decorating a 50th birthday in Ibadan. The celebrant says she wants something "classy and green". Her aso ebi is emerald green lace.
steps: Funke asks for a photo of the lace and sees it is a deep emerald.
She chooses a complementary-leaning scheme: emerald as the 30 percent, ivory as the 60 percent base, and gold as the 10 percent accent.
Ivory tablecloths and chair covers form the base; emerald runners and balloon clusters form the secondary colour.
Gold charger plates, candle holders and the "50" marquee number provide the accent.
The focal point is a backdrop of ivory drapes with an emerald and gold balloon garland behind the celebrant's chair.
blocks.result: The celebrant approves a mood board with three colours and one clear focal point, and her guests' emerald outfits match the room in photos.

blocks.text: Height, texture and repetition

Colour is only half of design. A table where every item is the same height looks flat, so mix one tall element (a candle stand or a tall vase), some medium pieces and some low ones. Mix textures too: shiny satin next to soft chiffon, matte balloons next to chrome ones, fresh leaves next to glass. Finally, **repeat** your key elements. The same flower or balloon cluster appearing at the entrance, the backdrop and the cake table ties the whole room together, and guests feel it even if they cannot say why.

Keep sightlines open on guest tables. Centrepieces should be either low, below about chin height when seated, or tall and slim so guests can talk across the table under them. A wide, medium-height arrangement blocks faces and usually gets moved to the floor by guests within an hour.

Always check colours in the light of the venue. A balloon that looks peach in daylight can look orange under warm hall bulbs. When you can, take a sample balloon or fabric swatch to the venue and look at it where it will hang.

takeaways: Limit yourself to about three colours and repeat them everywhere.
Use 60-30-10: main colour on big surfaces, accent on small details.
Choose one focal point and spend most effort there.
Check aso ebi fabric and venue lighting before confirming colours.

activity.title: Build two palettes
steps: Pick a real or imagined event: a child's birthday and a church thanksgiving.
For each, choose a scheme (monochrome, analogous or complementary) and write three colours.
Assign 60, 30 and 10 percent to specific items: cloths, runners, balloons, props.
Name the focal point for each event.
Collect three photos online or from your gallery that show each palette and save them as a mood board.
activity.evidence: Two simple mood boards (photo collage or screenshots) with colour names and 60-30-10 notes.

lessons.title: Your readiness, starter kit and core safety rules
objectives: Assess your skills, transport, helpers and time honestly
Write a starter kit list with approximate costs
State the core safety rules for candles, electrics, heights and fabric
Choose a first event type that fits your current capacity

blocks.text: Before taking money from a client, check that you can deliver on the day. Decoration fails less because of poor taste and more because of practical gaps: no transport, no helper, a missing extension cable, or setup starting two hours late. This lesson helps you see your gaps clearly and close them before your first paid job.

blocks.name: checklist
blocks.alt: A person ticking items on a checklist
blocks.caption: A short readiness checklist protects you from promising more than you can deliver.

blocks.text: Four readiness questions

items: **Skills:** Can you inflate and tie balloons evenly, build a garland, dress a table and drape fabric neatly? If not, which one will you practise first?
**Transport:** How will items reach the venue? A keke or small car works for a home birthday; a wedding may need a bus or pickup and two trips.
**People:** Who are your one or two reliable helpers, and are they free on Saturday mornings, when many events happen?
**Time:** Can you be at the venue early, sometimes the night before, and stay to pack down after the event?

blocks.text: A sensible starter kit

Buy tools first and decorations second. Tools are used at every job; trendy props may suit only one theme. Prices below are rough guides from Nigerian markets and online sellers, so confirm current prices before you budget.

head: Item
Why you need it
Approximate cost (₦)
rows: Saves time and breath; an electric pump is much faster for garlands
Balloon sizer or a cardboard template
Makes every balloon the same size
Holds fabric and garlands for photos
Garland strip, glue dots, fishing line, cable ties
Tape, scissors, pins, clips, step ladder
Fixing fabric and reaching heights safely
Extension box with surge protection, gaffer tape
Safe power for lights and pumps

blocks.title: Rent the big items at first
blocks.text: Chairs, tables, chair covers, large drapes and stage frames are usually rented from event rental companies. Own them only when you rent the same item often enough that buying is clearly cheaper. Module 2 shows how to work this out.
Core safety rules you will follow at every job
Decoration puts open flames, electricity, ladders and lots of flammable fabric in rooms full of people. Learn these rules now and treat them as non-negotiable.

blocks.title: Safety before guests arrive
items: Candles 12 inches from fabric
No overloaded extension boxes
Cables taped flat, away from water
Ladder held by a helper
Exits and walkways kept clear
Heavy pieces weighted or tied
blocks.caption: Walk the room with this checklist before you hand over to the client.

items: **Candles:** The US Fire Administration advises keeping candles at least 12 inches (about 30 cm) from anything that can burn, in stable holders where they cannot be knocked over. Near drapes, flowers or balloons, use battery-operated flameless candles instead.
**Electrics:** Do not plug one extension box into another. Keep cables taped down where people walk, away from drinks and water, and switch off lights you are adjusting.
**Generators:** Generators produce carbon monoxide, a poisonous gas you cannot smell. They must run outside, never inside a hall, canopy or closed room.
**Heights:** Use a proper step ladder, never a stacked chair, and have a helper hold it.
**Weight:** Backdrop stands and balloon arches catch wind outdoors. Weight their bases with sandbags or water weights and tie them to fixed points.

blocks.text: Fabric deserves special attention. Light materials such as chiffon, voile and organza catch fire easily and burn fast. Keep them well away from candles, hot halogen bulbs and generator exhausts, and never drape fabric directly over a hot light fitting. Ask your fabric supplier whether a material is flame-retardant; if they cannot say, treat it as flammable.

blocks.title: Know where the fire extinguisher is
blocks.text: At every venue, find the fire extinguisher and the exits before you start. If the venue has none, bring a small fire extinguisher whenever your design uses real candles or many electrical lights.

blocks.title: Worked example: a readiness check before saying yes
blocks.context: For example, Halima in Kaduna is asked to decorate a church harvest reception for 150 guests. She has done three home birthdays.
steps: Skills: she has never dressed 15 round tables, so she practises one table at home with a rented cloth and times herself: 12 minutes.
Time: 15 tables at 12 minutes is 180 minutes for one person, or about 90 minutes with a helper working in parallel.
Transport: her car cannot carry everything, so she books the rental company's delivery for tables and cloths.
Safety: the design uses real candles on tables, so she switches to flameless candles because the centrepieces include dried flowers.
blocks.result: Halima accepts the job with a clear plan, a helper booked and one safety risk removed, instead of discovering the gaps on the day.

takeaways: Practical gaps (transport, helpers, time) cause more failures than poor taste.
Buy tools first; rent big items until you rent them often.
Candles at least 12 inches from anything that burns, or go flameless.
Generators outside only; no extension box plugged into another.

activity.title: Write your readiness plan
steps: Answer the four readiness questions in writing: skills, transport, people, time.
List the starter kit items you already own and those you still need, with approximate prices from your local market.
Name the first event type you will offer, matched to your current capacity.
Copy the safety checklist into your phone notes so it is with you at every job.
activity.evidence: A one-page readiness plan with your kit list, gaps, chosen first event type and saved safety checklist.

quiz.q: A new decorator with two small birthday jobs behind her is offered a 400 guest wedding with ceiling draping next month. What is the wisest response?
options: Accept and learn on the day
Offer to join an experienced decorator's crew for this one, or decline politely
Accept but charge less in case it goes wrong
Accept and hire unknown helpers the night before
quiz.explain: Large jobs carry risks you cannot fix once guests arrive. Building experience under an established decorator protects the client and your reputation.

quiz.q: Using the 60-30-10 rule with ivory, emerald and gold, which item should carry the 60 percent?
quiz.explain: The main colour goes on the biggest surfaces, which in a hall are tablecloths, chair covers and drapes.

quiz.q: Gold, orange and burnt orange sit next to each other on the colour wheel. What kind of scheme is this?
quiz.explain: Colours that sit side by side on the wheel form an analogous scheme.

quiz.q: Your centrepieces include dried flowers and the client wants candlelight. What should you do?
options: Use tall real candles so the flame is above the flowers
Use real candles but blow them out after an hour
quiz.explain: Real flames near flammable material are a fire risk. Flameless candles give the look safely, as fire safety agencies recommend.

quiz.q: Where should a generator powering the event lights be placed?
options: Inside the hall near the stage
Under the canopy so it stays dry
Outside, away from the hall and canopy openings
quiz.explain: Generators produce carbon monoxide, which is poisonous and has no smell. They must run outside, away from where people gather.

modules.title: Guided practice: brief, build and price a decoration job
modules.overview: Work through a real job in order: take a proper client brief and venue check, learn the core building techniques (balloon garlands and arches, backdrops, fabric draping and table settings), then turn the design into a clear quotation with a deposit. You will decide what to rent and what to buy using simple numbers.

lessons.title: The client brief, venue check and design proposal
objectives: Run a client brief conversation using a written question list
Measure and photograph a venue so you can design accurately
Prepare a one-page design proposal with mood board and item list
Get the client's written approval before buying anything

blocks.text: Most decoration disputes start with words that meant different things to the client and the decorator: "elegant", "not too much", "gold". A **client brief** is a short, structured conversation that turns those words into specific decisions you both agree on. It protects your time, the client's money and your reputation.

blocks.name: conversation
blocks.caption: A good brief is a conversation with written answers, not a quick chat you try to remember later.

blocks.text: The brief questions
Ask these questions in person, on a call or by WhatsApp voice note, then send a written summary back so the client can confirm it. Keep the list in your phone and use it every time.

items: **The event:** type, date, start time, end time, and the time guests start arriving.
**The venue:** exact address, indoor or outdoor, contact person at the venue, earliest time you can enter, and when you must clear out.
**Guests:** expected number, and how many tables and what shape (round or rectangular).
**Look:** colours (with aso ebi or fabric photos), theme, three pictures they love and one they dislike.
**Zones:** which areas they want decorated: entrance, backdrop, stage or high table, guest tables, cake table, ceiling.
**Budget:** a range for decoration only, not the whole event.
**Rules:** anything the venue or church does not allow, such as nails, tape on walls, open flames or confetti.

blocks.title: Ask for one picture they dislike
blocks.text: Clients often struggle to explain what they want, but they know immediately what they do not want. One disliked picture can save you from a whole wrong direction.
The venue check

Visit the venue if you can, or ask the client or venue manager for a slow walk-through video. Measure with a tape measure and write numbers down. You need: the room length and width, the ceiling height, the backdrop wall width, the size and position of the stage, the number and size of tables, door widths for carrying in large pieces, and the location of power sockets. Note the light: warm yellow bulbs, white fluorescent tubes or daylight all change how colours look.

Photograph each wall and corner, the ceiling and any fixed hooks or beams. Ask the venue manager who supplies chairs and tables, whether they provide covers, whether there is a generator and who runs it, and whether another event is booked in the hall before yours. A morning wedding in the same hall can cut your setup window in half.

blocks.title: From brief to approved design
items: Brief questions answered
Venue measured and photographed
Mood board and sketch
Item list and quotation
Client approves in writing
blocks.caption: Nothing is bought or rented until the last box is ticked.

blocks.text: The design proposal

Keep the proposal to one or two pages so it is easy to read on a phone. Include a **mood board** (six to nine photos showing the colours and style), a simple **sketch** of the main focal point with measurements, a **zone list** describing each area in one line, and the **quotation** (covered in lesson 3 of this module). Free apps such as Canva let you build a mood board and export it as an image or PDF to send on WhatsApp.

blocks.title: Worked example: a church anniversary brief
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Port Harcourt is contacted by a church women's fellowship for its 25th anniversary reception in the church hall: 120 guests, Saturday 12 noon, colours royal blue and silver.
steps: Brief: guests arrive from 11:30 am; the hall is free from 7:00 am; the church does not allow nails or open flames; budget for decor is about ₦350,000 to ₦450,000 (approximate).
Venue check: hall is 18 m by 12 m, ceiling 4 m, stage 6 m wide. There are 12 round tables of 1.5 m (60 inches), seating 10 each.

Design: silver-white base cloths, royal blue runners, low silver centrepieces with white flowers, and a stage backdrop of white drapes with a royal blue and silver balloon garland and "25" marquee numbers.
Constraint applied: flameless candles only, and all fabric fixed with clips and cable ties to the stage frame, not nailed.
She sends a one-page proposal with mood board, sketch and quotation, and the fellowship leader replies "approved" on WhatsApp.
blocks.result: Grace has a written, approved design that respects the church's rules, fits the room's real measurements and gives her a clear setup window of 7:00 am to 11:00 am.

blocks.text: If the client changes something after approval, such as adding a ceiling drape or switching colours, update the proposal and the price, and get a fresh written "yes". Small verbal changes pile up, and on the day nobody remembers who agreed to what.
Save the brief summary, venue photos and the client's approval message in one folder for each job. If anything is disputed later, you have a clear record of what was agreed.

takeaways: Turn vague words into written decisions with a fixed brief question list.
Measure the venue and note sockets, light and access times.
Send a short proposal: mood board, sketch, zones and quotation.
Buy nothing until the client approves in writing.

activity.title: Run a practice brief
steps: Copy the brief questions into your phone notes.
Interview a friend or relative about a real or planned event using every question.
Measure one room (your sitting room or church hall) and note the measurements and socket positions.
Build a simple mood board in Canva or a photo collage app.
Write a one-page proposal and ask your practice client to approve or comment.
activity.evidence: Your completed brief notes, room measurements and one-page proposal saved as a PDF or screenshots.

lessons.title: Building the pieces: balloon garlands, backdrops, draping and tables
objectives: Build an organic balloon garland and estimate balloons by test-building
Calculate tablecloth size from table diameter and drop
Plan backdrop fabric width using a fullness ratio
Set a guest table neatly and consistently

blocks.text: Clients see the finished room; your skill is in the building. This lesson covers the four pieces that appear at almost every Nigerian event: balloon work, backdrops, fabric draping and table settings. Practise each at home before using it on a paid job.

blocks.name: balloon
blocks.caption: Balloon work is often the first thing guests photograph, so even sizing matters.

blocks.text: Balloon garlands and arches

Latex balloons are commonly sold in sizes such as 5 inch, 11 inch and 18 inch. An **organic garland** mixes these sizes for a natural, cloud-like look. A **classic arch** uses clusters of balloons of one size in a regular pattern on a frame. For most beginners the organic garland is easier and more forgiving.

items: Inflate 11 inch balloons slightly under full size so they are rounder and less likely to burst. Use a sizer so they match.
Inflate a smaller number of 18 inch balloons for volume and many 5 inch balloons for filling gaps.
Tie two balloons together by their necks to make a pair, then twist two pairs together to make a cluster of four.
Push the knots through the holes of a balloon decorating strip, or twist clusters onto a strong line, rotating each cluster so the garland is round.
Attach the garland to the backdrop stand or frame with cable ties or fishing line, then add 18 inch and 5 inch balloons with glue dots to fill gaps.

blocks.title: Count by test-building
blocks.text: Do not guess balloon numbers. Build 30 cm (one foot) of garland in your chosen style, count the balloons, then multiply by the total length you need and add about 10 percent for bursts. Record the count for future quotes.

Air-filled garlands last much longer than helium balloons, which lose float within hours to a day. Sunlight makes latex cloudy and weak, so keep outdoor balloon work in shade where possible and set it up close to the event time. Some guests are allergic to latex; for an indoor event with a known allergy, use foil balloons and fabric instead. Keep foil balloons away from overhead power lines, as the metallic coating can conduct electricity.
Backdrops and fabric draping

A backdrop is usually an adjustable pipe frame with fabric panels hung from the top bar. To look full rather than flat, fabric needs **gathers**. Decorators commonly use 1.5 to 2 times the frame width in fabric. For a 3 m wide frame, that means about 4.5 m to 6 m of total fabric width. Satin gives shine, chiffon and voile give soft, see-through layers, and many decorators layer a solid fabric behind a sheer one.

Draping ceilings or walls needs secure anchor points and the venue's permission. Never hang fabric from light fittings, fans or electrical cables. If the hall has no safe fixing points, use free-standing frames instead.
Table settings

Tablecloth size comes from simple maths: **cloth diameter = table diameter + 2 × drop**. The drop is how far the cloth hangs down each side. A standard dining table is about 30 inches (76 cm) high, so a 30 inch drop reaches the floor.

blocks.title: Floor-length vs half-drop cloth
items: Floor-length
Half-drop
blocks.caption: Pick the drop to match the formality of the event and the budget.

blocks.title: Worked example: tablecloths for a reception
blocks.context: For example, Grace (from the previous lesson) has 12 round tables of 60 inches (about 1.5 m) and wants floor-length cloths.
steps: Cloth diameter = 60 + (2 × 30) = 120 inches.
She asks the rental company for 120 inch round cloths and orders 13, one spare in case of a stain.
Each table seats 10, so she needs 120 chair covers and sashes, plus about 5 spares.
For runners on 12 tables, she needs 12 runners plus 1 spare.
blocks.result: Grace places an exact rental order (13 cloths, 125 chair covers, 13 runners) instead of discovering on the day that her cloths stop halfway down the legs.

blocks.text: For each place setting, keep it consistent: plate or charger centred in front of the chair, napkin on the plate or to the left, cutlery in order of use from the outside in, and glasses above the knife on the right. Lay one sample table, photograph it, and have helpers copy the photo exactly.

Finish every table the same way: cloth centred with equal drop on all sides, runner straight along the middle, centrepiece exactly in the centre, and chairs pushed in evenly. Stand at the entrance and look across the room; any table that is slightly off stands out immediately in photos. Iron or steam cloths before laying them, or hang them on arrival, because creases show badly under hall lights and in pictures.

takeaways: Build a short test garland and count, then add about 10 percent.
Cloth diameter = table diameter + 2 × drop.
Use about 1.5 to 2 times the frame width in fabric for full backdrops.
Lay one sample table and have helpers copy its photo.

activity.title: Practise the four pieces
steps: Build 30 cm of organic garland and record how many balloons of each size you used.
Calculate the cloth size for a 72 inch round table with a floor-length drop.
Hang a piece of fabric on a curtain rod or frame using 1.5 times the width and photograph it.
Set one complete place setting and photograph it from above.
activity.evidence: Photos of your garland sample, fabric gathers and place setting, plus your written balloon count and cloth calculation.

lessons.title: Quotations, deposits and deciding what to rent or buy
objectives: Build a quotation that covers materials, rentals, labour, transport and profit
Set clear deposit and balance terms
Calculate the break-even point for buying instead of renting
Handle client requests to reduce the price without losing money

blocks.text: Many decorators work hard and still lose money because they price by feeling or by copying others. A **quotation** is a written price that lists what you will provide, what it costs and the terms of payment. Built properly, it covers every naira you spend, pays you for your time and leaves profit to grow the business.

blocks.name: receipt
blocks.caption: A clear, itemised quotation prevents arguments about what was included.

blocks.text: The six parts of a quotation

items: **Materials you use up:** balloons, flowers, glue dots, tape, printed signs.
**Rentals:** cloths, chair covers, frames, stands, lights.
**Wear on your own items:** a small charge for things you own, so you can replace them.
**Labour:** you and your helpers, including setup and pack-down hours.
**Transport:** trips to market, to the venue and back, and any delivery fees.
**Contingency and profit:** a buffer for price changes and breakages, then your profit margin.

blocks.title: Worked example: quoting a birthday (all prices approximate)
blocks.context: For example, Tolu in Lagos is quoting a 30th birthday at a small lounge: balloon garland backdrop, cake table, 6 guest tables with runners and centrepieces. Prices are rough illustrations; use your own market prices.
steps: Materials: balloons ₦28,000, fresh flowers ₦40,000, glue dots, ties and tape ₦6,000, printed sign ₦12,000. Total ₦86,000.
Rentals: backdrop frame and drape ₦25,000, 6 runners ₦9,000, cake table cloth ₦5,000. Total ₦39,000.
Wear on own items (pump, stands, holders): ₦10,000.
Labour: Tolu plus 2 helpers for 6 hours including pack-down; helpers at ₦10,000 each, Tolu's design and supervision ₦30,000. Total ₦50,000.
Transport: market trips and bus to venue and back ₦20,000.
Subtotal ₦205,000. Contingency at 10 percent: ₦20,500. Running total ₦225,500.
Profit at 25 percent of ₦225,500: about ₦56,400. Quote rounded to ₦282,000.
blocks.result: Tolu sends a quotation of ₦282,000 with each zone listed. Every cost is covered, she is paid for her work, and there is real profit, not just a busy weekend.

blocks.text: Deposits and payment terms

Never buy or rent for a client without a deposit. The deposit covers what you must spend in advance and shows the client is committed. Many decorators ask for a large part upfront, for example 50 to 70 percent on approval, with the balance paid a few days before the event, not after it. Write your terms on the quotation: deposit amount, balance due date, what happens if the client cancels (for example, the deposit covers costs already spent), and how many days the quotation is valid, since market prices change. Send a short receipt or acknowledgement message for every payment you receive, showing the amount, the date and the balance still due.

blocks.title: Payment scams
blocks.text: Only accept a payment as received when it shows in your bank or wallet app, such as Opay or Moniepoint. Screenshots of "successful" transfers can be faked. A payment link from Paystack or your bank also gives the client a clear receipt.
Rent or buy?

Buy an item only when renting it repeatedly would cost more. Divide the purchase price by what you pay to rent it each time. The answer is the number of uses to **break even**. Also consider storage space, cleaning and transport: a stack of 100 chair covers needs washing, ironing and dry storage.

blocks.title: What to own and what to rent
items: Buy: used often, cheap to store
Buy later: used often, bulky
Rent: rarely used, cheap
Always rent: rare and bulky
blocks.caption: Own the small, frequently used items first; leave bulky, rarely used items to rental companies.

blocks.text: If a client says your quote is too high, reduce **scope**, not your profit. Offer to remove the ceiling draping, use artificial instead of fresh flowers, or decorate fewer zones. Show the new total. Cutting your margin to win a job teaches clients that your first price was not real.
Presenting the quotation

Send the quotation as a clean PDF or image with your business name, phone number, the client's name, event date and venue at the top. List each zone with what it includes, for example "Backdrop: 3 m white satin and chiffon drape, organic balloon garland in blue and silver, 25 marquee numbers". Clients compare quotes, and a detailed one shows exactly what they get for the money. Avoid one-line quotes such as "Full decoration: ₦400,000"; they invite arguments about what was included.
Keep a copy of every quotation, even those that are not accepted. Over time they show you which price ranges clients accept for each event type, and they make the next quote faster to prepare.

takeaways: Quote materials, rentals, wear, labour, transport, contingency and profit.
Take a deposit before spending; collect the balance before the event.
Break-even uses = buy price ÷ rent price per event.
Cut scope, not profit, when a client asks for a lower price.

activity.title: Price a real job
steps: Use the design from your practice brief in lesson 1.
Get real prices for materials and rentals from at least two local sellers or rental companies.
Build a quotation using all six parts, with 10 percent contingency and your chosen profit margin.
Write your deposit, balance and cancellation terms at the bottom.
Calculate the break-even uses for one item you are thinking of buying.
activity.evidence: A completed quotation (spreadsheet or document) with terms, plus your break-even calculation.

quiz.q: A client wants floor-length cloths for 72 inch round tables that are 30 inches high. What cloth diameter should you order?
quiz.explain: Cloth diameter = table diameter + 2 × drop = 72 + 60 = 132 inches.

quiz.q: You built 30 cm of organic garland using 14 balloons. The backdrop needs a 3 m garland. About how many balloons should you plan for?
quiz.explain: 3 m is 10 × 30 cm, so 14 × 10 = 140 balloons, plus about 10 percent for bursts, which is about 154 to 155.

quiz.q: A backdrop frame costs ₦60,000 to buy and ₦10,000 to rent per event. After how many uses does buying break even?
quiz.explain: Break-even uses = buy price ÷ rent price = 60,000 ÷ 10,000 = 6.

quiz.q: A client says your ₦300,000 quote is too high. What is the best response?
options: Drop to ₦220,000 and hope to save on materials
Offer a smaller scope, such as removing ceiling draping, with a new total
Agree to the lower price but use fewer balloons without telling her
quiz.explain: Reducing scope keeps your pricing honest and profitable, and the client chooses what to give up.

quiz.q: Which question is most important to ask the venue during your check?
options: What colour the walls were last year
The earliest time you can enter and whether another event is in the hall before yours
How many weddings they hosted this year
quiz.explain: Your setup window decides your whole timeline and crew size. An earlier event in the hall can cut it sharply.

quiz.q: A client sends a screenshot of a ₦150,000 deposit transfer, but nothing shows in your Moniepoint app yet. What should you do?
options: Wait until the money shows in your account before spending
Book the rentals and sort it later
quiz.explain: Screenshots can be faked. Treat a payment as received only when it appears in your own bank or wallet app.

modules.title: Quality and evidence: logistics, on-site safety and records
modules.overview: Plan the event day backwards from the guests' arrival, set up to a clear quality standard and hand over a safe room. Then learn the honest business practices and simple records that turn each job into evidence of your reliability and a guide for pricing the next one.

lessons.title: Logistics, setup timelines and the final walkthrough
objectives: Build a setup timeline by working backwards from guest arrival
Prepare a packing list and load plan for transport
Assign crew roles so setup runs in parallel
Carry out a final walkthrough against a quality standard

blocks.text: On the event day you are racing a clock you do not control. Guests arrive when the invitation says, not when you finish. Good decorators plan the day **backwards**: start with the moment the room must be ready, then subtract each task, travel time and a buffer, until you reach the time you must leave home.

blocks.name: time-management
blocks.alt: A person organising tasks against a clock
blocks.caption: Plan backwards from guest arrival, then protect a buffer for surprises.

blocks.text: Working backwards

items: Write the **ready time**: at least 30 to 60 minutes before guests are expected, because early guests, photographers and the client will arrive before the official time.
List every setup task with a time estimate from your practice sessions, such as tables, backdrop, balloon garland, entrance and cake table.
Decide which tasks run in parallel, with different crew members working at the same time.
Add a buffer of about 20 to 25 percent of the setup time for late deliveries, a locked hall or a missing item.
Add loading time and travel time, allowing for traffic on a Saturday morning in your city.

blocks.title: Worked example: timeline for a 12 noon reception
blocks.context: For example, Grace's church anniversary reception starts at 12:00, guests from 11:30. The hall opens at 7:00. Her crew is Grace plus three helpers.
steps: Ready time: 11:00, giving a 30 minute margin before guests.
Tasks: tables and chair covers 90 minutes (two helpers), backdrop drape and garland 120 minutes (Grace and one helper), centrepieces 45 minutes, entrance 30 minutes, final walkthrough 15 minutes.
Parallel plan: backdrop runs from 7:30 to 9:30 while tables run from 7:30 to 9:00; centrepieces from 9:30 to 10:15; entrance 9:00 to 9:30; buffer 10:15 to 10:45; walkthrough 10:45 to 11:00.
Before 7:30: arrive 7:00, unload and sort items by zone for 30 minutes.
Load the bus at 5:45; travel 45 minutes with Saturday traffic; leave by 6:15.
blocks.result: Grace knows to leave home by 6:15, has a 30 minute buffer built in and finishes her walkthrough at 11:00, a full 30 minutes before the first guests.

blocks.title: Event morning at a glance
items: 6:15 Leave with loaded bus
7:00 Arrive, unload, sort
7:30 Backdrop and tables
9:30 Centrepieces and entrance
10:45 Final walkthrough
11:00 Room ready
blocks.caption: Every time on the day comes from working backwards from the ready time.

blocks.text: Packing and loading

Pack by **zone**, not by item type. Put everything for the cake table in one crate labelled "Cake table", everything for the backdrop in another, and keep a separate "tools" crate with scissors, tape, cable ties, glue dots, pins, flameless candles with spare batteries, extension box and a small first aid kit. Tick each crate off a packing list as it goes into the vehicle, and again when it comes out. Load the items you need first last, so they come out first.

blocks.title: Inflate early, but not too early
blocks.text: Air-filled garlands can often be built the evening before and transported in large bags. Helium balloons should be inflated as close to the event as possible, because they lose float within hours.
Crew roles

Give each helper a clear job and a photo of what the finished zone should look like. One person leads tables, one leads the backdrop, and you move between zones checking quality and solving problems. Avoid having everyone wait for you to give instructions; that wastes the most valuable hour of the morning.

Agree helpers' pay, arrival time and food before the day, and share the run sheet with them on WhatsApp the evening before. Confirm deliveries the day before too: call the rental company to confirm the number of cloths and chair covers, the delivery time and the exact address. Save the venue contact's number and the client's agreed contact person in your phone, because the bride or celebrant should not be the one answering decoration questions on the morning of her event.

Keep a small **emergency kit** in your tools crate: spare balloons in every colour you are using, extra cable ties, a second roll of tape, safety pins, a needle and thread, a small steamer or travel iron if the venue has power, and a phone power bank. Most morning crises are solved by one of these items.
The final walkthrough standard

items: **Matches the approval:** colours, zones and focal point are what the client approved.
**Secure:** stands weighted, garlands tied, nothing leaning; give each piece a gentle shake.
**Safe:** walkways and exits clear, cables taped, candles flameless or safely spaced.
**Neat:** equal tablecloth drops, no creases, no visible tape or ties, no balloon scraps on the floor.
**Clean:** packaging, offcuts and empty bags removed from the hall.

blocks.text: Take photos of every zone before guests arrive, while the room is empty and tidy. These become your portfolio pictures and your proof of what you delivered. Then hand over to the client or venue contact and tell them who to call if something needs attention during the event.

takeaways: Plan backwards from a ready time 30 to 60 minutes before guests.
Run tasks in parallel and add a 20 to 25 percent buffer.
Pack by zone and tick crates in and out.
Walk through for match, security, safety, neatness and cleanliness, then photograph.

activity.title: Write your event-day run sheet
steps: Take the job from your Module 2 practice brief.
Set a ready time and list all tasks with time estimates.
Assign tasks to crew members and mark which run in parallel.
Add a buffer, loading and travel time, and write your leave-home time.
Write a packing list grouped by zone, plus your tools crate.
activity.evidence: A one-page run sheet with timeline, crew roles and packing list.

lessons.title: On-site safety, honest dealing and handling things that go wrong
objectives: Identify and control the main hazards in a decorated venue
Make outdoor decor stable in wind and sun
Communicate changes and substitutions honestly
Respond calmly to common event-day problems

blocks.text: Decorated rooms are full of things that can hurt people: open flames, hot lights, long cables, tall frames and lots of flammable fabric. Your name is attached to every piece you install. A safe room and honest dealing are part of quality, not extras.

blocks.name: fire-extinguisher
blocks.caption: Know where the extinguisher is before you light or plug in anything.

blocks.text: The main hazards and their controls

head: Hazard
What can happen
Control
rows: Fabric, flowers or hair catch fire
Keep at least 12 inches (30 cm) from anything that burns, in stable holders; use flameless candles near fabric or where children are
One extension box per wall socket, no daisy-chaining, total load within the box's rating
Guests trip, equipment is pulled down
Route along walls; tape flat with gaffer tape or use cable covers
Weight bases, tie to fixed points, check before guests arrive
Keep a gap between bulbs and fabric; prefer LED lights, which run cooler
Run generators outside, away from doors, windows and canopies

blocks.title: Safety routine at every job
items: Spot hazards at venue check
Plan controls in the design
Install safely
Inspect before handover
Note lessons after event
blocks.caption: Safety is a loop you repeat at every job, not a single check.

blocks.text: Outdoor events

Many Nigerian events happen under canopies on compounds or in gardens. Wind is the main enemy. Weight every stand with sandbags or water weights, tie arches to fixed posts or stakes, and avoid large flat panels that act like sails. Keep balloons in shade where you can, since direct sun weakens latex and makes it cloudy. In the rainy season, ask the client about tents and keep fabrics and electrics well clear of rainwater runoff.

blocks.title: Children at the party
blocks.text: At children's events, keep small burst balloon pieces off the floor, since they are a choking hazard for young children. Pick up bursts immediately and keep uninflated balloons out of reach.
Honest dealing

Things change between quotation and event day: a flower is out of season, a rental company runs out of gold chairs, a fabric colour arrives slightly different. Tell the client as soon as you know, explain the option you recommend and any price difference, and get agreement in writing. A silent substitution, discovered on the day, damages trust more than the change itself.

Be honest about capacity too. If you are offered two events on the same Saturday and your crew can only handle one properly, decline the second or refer it to a decorator you trust. A client's wedding happens once; doing it badly because you overbooked is not recoverable.

Honesty also covers your marketing. Only post photos of work you actually did, and say clearly when a picture is inspiration rather than your own setup. If you worked as part of another decorator's crew, credit them. Clients who book you because of borrowed photos will be disappointed on the day, and in a city where vendors talk to each other, that story travels quickly.
Common event-day problems

items: **Hall still in use:** confirm the handover time in writing the day before and plan a shorter setup with more helpers if needed.
**Late rental delivery:** start with zones that use your own items, such as the backdrop and balloons, while you chase the delivery.
**Balloons bursting in heat:** under-inflate slightly, keep spares, and keep balloons away from direct sun and hot lights.

blocks.title: Worked example: a problem on the day
blocks.context: For example, Amaka in Abuja arrives at a hotel for a 4 pm wedding reception and finds the hall's ceiling hooks, which she planned to use for draping, have been removed during renovations.
steps: She stops and checks the time: setup started at 9:00, ready time is 3:00, so she has six hours.
She drops the ceiling drape, which needs safe anchor points, rather than improvising from light fittings.
She moves the drape fabric to two extra backdrop frames placed either side of the high table, making the focal point wider and fuller.
She calls the bride's sister, the agreed contact, explains the change and the reason, and offers a partial refund for the ceiling draping as listed on the quotation.
She notes in her records to confirm fixing points again 48 hours before every future ceiling job.
blocks.result: The room is safe, the focal point is stronger, the client heard about the change before seeing it, and Amaka keeps both her reputation and the referral.

blocks.text: After the event, pack down as carefully as you set up. Remove every cable tie, clip and piece of tape, return the venue to the condition you found it, and count rented items against your rental list so nothing is lost or charged to you.

takeaways: Control flames, electrics, cables, heights, hot lights and generator fumes.
Outdoors, weight and tie everything and keep balloons in shade.
Tell clients about changes early and agree in writing.
Never improvise fixings from lights or cables; change the design instead.

activity.title: Do a hazard check
steps: Visit a hall, church or room you might decorate.
List every hazard you can see: sockets, cables, light fittings, exits, wind exposure.
For each hazard, write the control you would use.
Write a short message you would send a client to explain a substitution honestly.
activity.evidence: Your written hazard list with controls and your sample substitution message.

lessons.title: Client feedback, job records and tracking your progress
objectives: Collect useful feedback from clients after each event
Keep a simple job record that compares quoted and actual costs
Track a few key measures across jobs
Use your records to improve timing and pricing

blocks.text: Each event is a lesson you have already paid for. Without records, the lesson disappears after the weekend. With a simple job record, you learn how long things really take, what each event really costs and which clients send you more work.

blocks.name: feedback
blocks.alt: A person giving feedback with stars and comments
blocks.caption: Short, specific client feedback is the raw material for better jobs and stronger marketing.

blocks.text: Asking for feedback

Send a short message one or two days after the event, when the client has rested but still remembers. Ask specific questions rather than "how was it?". Clients answer more honestly when questions are easy and specific.

items: On a scale of 1 to 5, how close was the decor to what you pictured?
Was anything not as you expected, on the day or in our communication?
Did guests comment on any part of the decor?
May I share photos of the decor (without your guests' faces) and a sentence from your message on my page?
Would you recommend me to a friend? Who might need a decorator soon?

blocks.title: Privacy and permission
blocks.text: Ask before posting photos that show the client, their family or guests, especially children. Many decorators photograph the room before guests arrive so they can share decor freely without showing people.

Treat negative feedback as useful information, not an attack. Thank the client, ask one follow-up question to understand exactly what went wrong, and reply with what you will change. If a mistake was clearly yours, such as a missing item that was on the quotation, offer a fair remedy. A calm, honest reply often turns an unhappy client into one who still recommends you because of how you handled it.

Watch the room during the event too, if you are staying or can return. Notice which zones guests photograph most, whether centrepieces were moved because they blocked views, and whether anything sagged or fell as the hall warmed up. These observations are often more honest than anything a polite client will tell you afterwards.
The job record

Keep one row per job in a notebook or a free spreadsheet such as Google Sheets. Record the date, event type, guest count, quoted price, actual costs, setup time planned and actual, crew size, client rating and whether a referral came from it. Add one line on what to do differently next time.

blocks.title: Worked example: reviewing three jobs
blocks.context: For example, Tolu reviews her last three birthday jobs in Lagos (amounts approximate).
steps: Job 1: quoted ₦282,000, actual costs ₦214,000, profit ₦68,000. Setup planned 4 hours, actual 4 hours 40 minutes.
Job 2: quoted ₦190,000, actual costs ₦176,000, profit ₦14,000. Fresh flower prices rose after she quoted. Setup 3 hours, actual 3 hours 30 minutes.
Job 3: quoted ₦350,000, actual costs ₦262,000, profit ₦88,000. Setup planned 5 hours, actual 5 hours 50 minutes.
Pattern 1: every setup ran 15 to 20 percent over plan, mostly on balloon garlands.
Pattern 2: Job 2's quote had no validity date, so the flower price rise came out of her profit.
blocks.result: Tolu adds 20 percent to garland time estimates, starts building garlands the night before, and adds "valid for 7 days" to every quotation.

blocks.text: Measures worth tracking
You do not need many numbers. A few, tracked honestly across every job, tell you whether the business is getting stronger.

blocks.title: Five numbers per job
items: Profit after all costs
Setup time: planned vs actual
Client rating out of 5
Referrals received
Items damaged or lost
blocks.caption: Five honest numbers per job are enough to steer your business.

blocks.text: **Profit** tells you whether your pricing works. **Setup time accuracy** tells you whether your timelines can be trusted. **Client rating** and **referrals** tell you whether people value your work enough to send others. **Damage and loss** tells you whether your packing and pack-down habits are costing money, since lost rental items are charged to you.

Look at your records every month. If profit per job is falling, check whether material prices have risen faster than your quotes. If setups always run late, build in more buffer or add a helper. If referrals are low despite good ratings, you may simply need to ask for them more directly. Change one habit at a time, then watch the next few jobs to see whether the number moves, so you know which change actually helped.

Keep your receipts with each job record. Photograph market receipts on the day, since paper ones fade and get lost, and save them in the job folder. When you later register your business or open a business account, a few months of tidy records also make it much easier to show what your business earns.

takeaways: Ask specific feedback questions one or two days after the event.
Record quoted price, actual costs, planned and actual setup time per job.
Track profit, timing, rating, referrals and losses.
Review monthly and change one habit based on the pattern.

activity.title: Start your job record
steps: Create a Google Sheet or notebook page with the columns from this lesson.
Enter any past events you decorated, even family ones, as accurately as you can.
Write your client feedback message template and save it in your phone.
Note one pattern you can already see and one change you will make.
activity.evidence: A screenshot or photo of your job record with at least one entry and your feedback message template.

quiz.q: Guests are expected at 2:00 pm. Setup needs 4 hours with parallel work, and you add a 1 hour buffer. You want the room ready 30 minutes before guests. When should setup start?
quiz.explain: Ready time is 1:30 pm. Subtract 4 hours of setup and 1 hour of buffer: 1:30 minus 5 hours is 8:30 am.

quiz.q: On arrival you find the ceiling hooks you planned to drape from are gone. What should you do?
options: Tie the fabric to the light fittings
Change the design to use free-standing frames and tell the client
Use the ceiling fan as an anchor
Skip the draping without mentioning it
quiz.explain: Light fittings and fans are not safe anchors. Change the design safely and tell the client, offering any fair adjustment.

quiz.q: Which packing method makes setup fastest?
options: All balloons in one crate, all fabric in another
Pack by zone, with a separate tools crate
Put everything loose in the vehicle
quiz.explain: Packing by zone means each crew member can carry one crate to their area and start immediately.

quiz.q: Your last four jobs all ran 20 percent over planned setup time. What is the best action?
options: Ignore it, since you still finished
Add more buffer or crew to future timelines
Charge clients for the extra time afterwards
quiz.explain: Records show your estimates are consistently short, so adjust future plans before it causes a late finish.

quiz.q: When is the best time to photograph your decor for your portfolio?
options: At the end of the event
After the final walkthrough, before guests arrive
quiz.explain: The room is complete, clean and empty, so photos show your work clearly without guests' faces.

quiz.q: A flower you quoted for is out of season. What should you do?
options: Use any flower and say nothing
Tell the client early, recommend an alternative and any price change, and get agreement in writing
quiz.explain: Early, honest communication with written agreement protects trust; silent substitutions damage it.

modules.title: Portfolio and impact: your project, your offer and your next 90 days
modules.overview: Bring everything together in one documented decoration project, real or fully planned. Then turn your work into a portfolio and clear service packages that win clients, and set a practical 90-day plan for growing your decoration business.

lessons.title: Building your decoration project file from brief to pack-down
objectives: Choose a suitable real or practice event for your final project
Assemble a complete project file with brief, design, quotation and run sheet
Document execution with planned versus actual results
Write an honest reflection that names specific improvements

blocks.text: Your final project is one decoration job documented from the first conversation to the last cable tie. It proves you can do the whole job, not just make something pretty. The best project is a real event: a family birthday, a church fellowship meeting, a friend's small party or a paid job. If no event is available, you can complete a fully planned project with real prices and a real venue.

blocks.name: design-process
blocks.alt: A person arranging design steps on a board
blocks.caption: Your project file shows every step of your process, not only the final photos.

blocks.text: Choosing the right event

Pick something small enough to do very well. A home birthday for 30 to 60 guests with a backdrop, cake table and a few guest tables is ideal. It uses every skill in this course (brief, colour scheme, balloon work, table setting, quotation, logistics, safety and feedback) without overwhelming you. If you are doing it for family or a friend at no charge, still prepare a full quotation so you practise pricing.

Treat a family job exactly like a paid one. Run the full brief, even with your sister. Agree the design in writing, even if the "approval" is a WhatsApp thumbs-up. Set a ready time and stick to it. Family events are where many decorators get careless, and they are also where many first paying clients see your work, because guests ask "who did the decoration?".
What goes in the project file

blocks.title: Project file contents
items: Client brief and venue notes
Mood board and sketch
Quotation with payment terms
Run sheet and packing list
Before, during, after photos
Feedback and reflection
blocks.caption: Six sections, each one drawn from a module of this course.

items: **Client brief and venue notes:** the completed question list, room measurements, socket positions and venue rules.
**Design:** mood board, colour scheme with 60-30-10 notes, focal point sketch with measurements, and zone list.
**Quotation:** all six cost parts, contingency, profit, deposit and balance terms, and the client's approval message.
**Logistics:** run sheet with ready time, tasks, crew, buffer and leave-home time; packing list by zone; rental order.
**Execution evidence:** photos of the empty room, setup in progress, each finished zone, and the room after pack-down.
**Review:** client feedback, your job record row, and a written reflection.

blocks.title: Photograph the empty room first
blocks.text: A "before" photo of the bare hall makes your "after" photo far more impressive and proves the transformation is your work.
Planned versus actual

The most valuable part of your file is the comparison between what you planned and what happened. Make a short table: planned cost versus actual cost, planned setup time versus actual, items planned versus items used. Differences are not failures; they are information. A reviewer, or a future client, is more impressed by a decorator who knows exactly where her plan was off than by one who claims everything went perfectly.

blocks.title: Worked example: a planned versus actual table
blocks.context: For example, Blessing in Benin City decorates her niece's 10th birthday for 45 guests as her final project (amounts approximate).
steps: Quoted total ₦180,000; actual costs ₦139,000, so profit would have been ₦41,000 on a paid job.
Planned setup 3 hours with one helper; actual 3 hours 35 minutes, because the garland took longer than in practice.
Planned 160 balloons; used 148, with 9 bursts in the afternoon heat.
Planned real candles on the cake table; switched to flameless after seeing the paper backdrop sat close behind it.
Client feedback: rated 5 out of 5; guests loved the photo backdrop, but the cake table looked bare from the side.
blocks.result: Blessing's reflection names three specific changes: build garlands the night before, keep 10 percent spare balloons in hot weather, and dress cake tables on all visible sides.

blocks.text: Writing the reflection

Answer four questions in plain sentences. What went well, and why? What took longer or cost more than planned, and why? What did you adapt on the day, and was it the right decision? What will you do differently next time? Keep it honest and specific. "It was nice" teaches you nothing; "The garland took 35 minutes longer because I sized balloons by eye" tells you exactly what to fix.

If your project was planned but not executed, add a section explaining what you would check on the day and which risks worry you most. Use real prices from at least two sellers and a real venue you have measured, so the plan could genuinely be carried out tomorrow.

Organise the file so someone else can follow it. Put the sections in the order of the job, name the photos clearly (for example "03-backdrop-finished"), and export the whole thing as one PDF from Canva, Google Docs or your phone's notes app. A tidy file is itself evidence of the organised, reliable working style that clients pay for.

takeaways: Choose a small event you can do very well.
Your file has six sections: brief, design, quotation, logistics, photos, review.
Compare planned and actual for cost, time and materials.
Write a specific, honest reflection with concrete changes.

activity.title: Assemble your project file
steps: Choose your project event and confirm the date with the client.
Create a folder on your phone or Google Drive with the six section names.
Fill each section as you go, starting with the brief and venue notes.
After the event, complete the planned versus actual table and the reflection.
Export everything as one PDF.
activity.evidence: Your complete project file as a single PDF with all six sections.

lessons.title: Portfolio, packages and explaining your value to clients
objectives: Build a portfolio that shows range, quality and reliability
Design two or three service packages with clear inclusions
Explain your value using specific, evidence-based statements
Use WhatsApp Business tools to present your work professionally

blocks.text: Clients cannot touch your decor before they book. They decide based on what they see and how you talk about your work. A good portfolio and clear packages do most of the selling for you, and they let you spend less time answering the same questions.

blocks.name: portfolio
blocks.alt: A person presenting a portfolio of work
blocks.caption: Real photos of your own work are your strongest sales tool.

blocks.text: What a strong portfolio contains

items: **Your best 10 to 20 photos,** not every photo you have ever taken. Quality beats quantity.
**Range:** at least one birthday, one formal event (wedding or church) and one outdoor or canopy setup if you have them.
**Before and after pairs** showing the empty room and the finished space.
**Detail shots:** a close-up of a centrepiece, a balloon cluster, neat fabric gathers.
**Short captions:** event type, guest count, colours and one line about the challenge you solved.
**Client words:** a sentence from a feedback message, with permission.

blocks.text: Take portfolio photos in good light, straight on and from the entrance, with clutter removed. Turn off flash where possible and use the room's lights. Shoot the same zone from two or three angles. Your phone camera is enough if you keep the lens clean and hold steady.
Service packages

Packages make it easy for clients to choose and easy for you to quote. Base each package on your real costs from your job records, then add contingency and profit as you learned in Module 2. Always show what is included, so clients compare like with like.

head: Package
Includes
Example starting price (₦, approx.)
rows: Balloon garland on backdrop stand, cake table styling, welcome sign; up to 50 guests; home or small venue
Backdrop with drape and garland, cake table, up to 8 guest tables with runners and centrepieces, entrance
Full hall: stage or high table, backdrop, all guest tables, chair covers, entrance, ceiling or wall drape where safe

blocks.title: Prices are examples only
blocks.text: These figures illustrate the structure. Set your own prices from your costs, your city and your experience. Prices in Lagos or Abuja and in a smaller town can differ a lot, and market prices change often.

blocks.title: Vague vs specific value statements
items: Vague
Specific
blocks.caption: Specific statements backed by evidence build trust faster than adjectives.

blocks.text: Explaining your value

When a client asks why they should choose you, answer with facts. Describe your process: "I visit or video-check the venue, send a written design and quotation, plan the setup backwards from guest arrival, and finish with a safety walkthrough." Show proof: photos, a client message, your planned versus actual record. Be honest about your experience level. If an event is bigger than anything you have done, say so and explain how you will manage it, for example by hiring an experienced crew lead.

blocks.title: Worked example: replying to a price-shopper
blocks.context: For example, Zainab in Kano receives a message: "How much for birthday decoration?" with no other details.
steps: She replies warmly and sends her three-package catalogue image from WhatsApp Business.
She asks three brief questions: date, venue and approximate guest count.
The client chooses Classic Party for 70 guests, so Zainab notes it is just over the package limit and quotes ₦395,000 (approximate), listing the two extra tables.
She attaches four photos of similar past setups and one short client testimonial.
She states her terms: 60 percent deposit to confirm the date, balance three days before the event.
blocks.result: Instead of a bare price that invites comparison, the client receives a clear offer with proof and terms, and books the same day.

blocks.text: **WhatsApp Business** is a free app with a business profile, a catalogue for your packages, quick replies for common questions and labels to track enquiries. Set up a catalogue item for each package with photos and inclusions. Create quick replies for your brief questions and payment terms so every client gets a consistent, professional response.

Use labels such as "new enquiry", "quote sent", "deposit paid" and "completed" to see at a glance where each client stands. Follow up politely on quotes after two or three days; many clients simply forget to reply while juggling other vendors.
Keep your portfolio fresh

Add your best new photos after every job and remove weaker old ones, so the portfolio always shows your current standard. Post on WhatsApp Status and Instagram on the day after an event, when the client and guests are still talking about it, and tag vendors you worked with if they agree. Over time, group photos by event type in Instagram highlights or WhatsApp catalogue collections, so a mother planning a child's birthday sees only birthday work and a church committee sees only church receptions.

takeaways: Show 10 to 20 of your best real photos with range and before-and-after pairs.
Build packages from your real costs, with inclusions listed.
Explain value with your process and evidence, not adjectives.
Use WhatsApp Business catalogues and quick replies to stay consistent.

activity.title: Build your portfolio and packages
steps: Select your best 10 photos and write a short caption for each.
Draft two or three packages with inclusions and prices based on your costs.
Set up a WhatsApp Business profile and add each package to the catalogue.
Write three specific value statements backed by evidence from your work.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of your WhatsApp Business catalogue, your package list and your 10 captioned photos.

lessons.title: Final evidence check, certification and your 90-day growth plan
objectives: Check your project evidence against the certificate requirements
Set three measurable goals for the next 90 days
Plan your next skill to learn and your next equipment purchase
Take simple steps to formalise your business

blocks.text: You have learned how to take a brief, design with colour and focal points, build balloon work, backdrops and tables, quote with deposits, plan logistics, work safely and keep records. This final lesson checks that your evidence is complete and helps you plan the next three months so the skill turns into steady work.

blocks.name: certification
blocks.caption: Your certificate reflects real, documented decoration work.

blocks.text: Evidence check before the final quiz

items: A documented plan with the client's vision, budget, colour scheme and materials list.
A quotation with all cost parts, deposit and balance terms.
A run sheet with ready time, crew roles and buffer.
Photos of real execution (before, during, after), or a detailed, realistic plan using a real venue and real prices.
An honest reflection on setup timing, adaptations made and client feedback.

blocks.text: If any item is thin, strengthen it now. A certificate supported by real photos and real numbers carries far more weight with clients than one supported by a plan alone. If your project was planned only, look for a small real event in the next few weeks and add it to your file.
Your 90-day plan

Ninety days is long enough to complete several jobs and short enough to stay focused. Choose three goals you can measure. Good goals name a number and a date, such as "decorate four paid events by the end of the quarter" or "get three written client testimonials".

blocks.title: A sample 90-day plan
items: Days 1 to 30: portfolio and packages live
Days 31 to 60: two paid events
Days 61 to 90: two more events, review
blocks.caption: Build your foundations first, then do and review real jobs.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 90-day plan
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma in Owerri has completed her final project, a cousin's birthday, and wants paid work.
steps: Days 1 to 30: posts her project photos, sets up WhatsApp Business with two packages, and introduces herself to two cake makers and one event hall manager.
Days 31 to 60: decorates two paid birthdays and records both in her job sheet.
Days 61 to 90: decorates two more events, including her first church reception, working with one regular helper.
She saves part of the profit from each job towards an electric balloon pump, since her records show she rents or borrows one every time.
On day 90 she reviews her five numbers: profit per job, setup time accuracy, ratings, referrals and losses.
blocks.result: Ifeoma ends the quarter with four paid events, a stronger portfolio, a regular helper, her own pump and real data to set next quarter's prices.

blocks.text: Your next skill and next purchase

Choose one skill to deepen next, based on what clients ask for most in your area: classic balloon arches, fresh flower centrepieces, ceiling draping, lighting, or themed children's parties. Practise it at home, then offer it at a small job before advertising it. Choose your next equipment purchase using the break-even method from Module 2: buy what you rent most often, not what looks impressive.

Keep learning from others too. Offer to help an experienced decorator on a large wedding, even for modest pay, to see how big crews, ceiling work and lighting are managed. Watch tutorials from established decorators and balloon artists, then practise the technique at home before you sell it. Save part of each job's profit in a separate equipment fund, so growth is paid for by the business rather than borrowed.

Protect your energy as well. Saturdays can be long, starting before dawn and ending after pack-down late at night. Plan rest after big jobs, share lifting with helpers, carry water and food, and do not book back-to-back events until you have a crew you can trust.
Formalising your business

As work grows, a few steps make you look and work more professionally. Open a separate account for business money so you can see real profit. Choose a business name and check it is not already in use, then consider registering it with the **Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC)**, which offers business name registration online. A registered name helps when hotels, churches or companies ask for an invoice from a business. Keep using written quotations, deposits and job records at every event.

blocks.title: Build vendor partnerships
blocks.text: Event planners, caterers, cake makers, photographers and hall managers meet clients before decorators do. Deliver well on a shared event, then ask if they would be happy to recommend you, and recommend them back.

The difference between someone with good taste and a professional decorator is reliability: arriving early, building safely, delivering what was agreed and leaving the venue clean. Keep practising, keep records, and let every event become evidence for the next one.

takeaways: Check all five evidence items before the final quiz.
Set three measurable 90-day goals with numbers and dates.
Pick your next skill by client demand and your next purchase by break-even.
Separate business money and consider CAC business name registration.

activity.title: Write your 90-day plan
steps: Tick off each evidence item and fix any gaps in your project file.
Write three measurable goals for the next 90 days.
Name one skill to deepen and one item to buy, with the reason from your records.
List three vendors you will contact in the next two weeks.
activity.evidence: A one-page 90-day plan with goals, next skill, next purchase and vendor list, plus your completed evidence checklist.

quiz.q: Which project is the best choice for a first final project?
options: A 500 guest wedding at a hotel
A home birthday for about 40 guests with backdrop, cake table and a few tables
Only a mood board with no event
quiz.explain: A small event uses every skill in the course while staying manageable enough to do very well and document fully.
